stances.claim: The PH and US 2016 electoral landscapes both demonstrate the 'macho power vs woman power' phenomenon -- Duterte/Marcos and Trump are strong-willed, hyperbolic, magnetic, unorthodox, and brash; Poe/Robredo and Clinton are polished, compassionate, motherly, loving, and humble -- making this dichotomy a transnational pattern observable in two democracies simultaneously.
stances.rhetorical_move: transnational-pattern identification with five-trait contrast catalogs

stances.claim: The candidate-quotation comparison method -- using direct quotes on peace/order, corruption, poverty alleviation, foreign relations, and women -- allows readers to evaluate the macho-woman contrast on substantive policy positions rather than mere style, with Duterte's bloody-killing language and 'jet ski' Spratlys bravado contrasted against Poe's mother-and-child empathy register and constructive-engagement framework.
stances.rhetorical_move: direct-quotation comparison method with policy-domain categories

stances.claim: The Marcos-Robredo VP race exhibits parallel macho-woman contrasts: Marcos seeks to 'unite, not divide' and 'look to the future, not to the past' with aspiration to run DOLE for employment; Robredo identifies herself as 'a mother' refusing to abandon children or country, aspiring to streamline anti-poverty programs rather than hold cabinet position.

notable_anecdotes: The CJ-coined contrast: 'macho power vs woman power' -- used as both column title and analytical frame, capturing the 2016 electoral phenomenon in three words.
The transnational symmetry observation: Trump-Clinton 'Uncannily, they also typify the phenomenon of macho power vs woman power' -- making the PH pattern visible as part of a global moment.
Duterte's 'if I fail, kill me' self-stake -- preserved verbatim as the column's most extreme example of his macho-hyperbolic register.

Duterte's jet-ski Spratlys vow: 'Bababa ako, sasakay ako ng jet ski, dala-dala ko yung flag ng Pilipino at pupunta ako doon sa airport nila tapos itanim ko' -- preserved with Tagalog-to-English translation, capturing the unrealistic-bravado register that defined his campaign.

The Duterte rape comment quoted in full with Tagalog + translation: 'Sayang. Ang nagpasok sa isip ko, ni-rape nila, pinagpilahan nila doon. Nagalit ako kasi ni-rape, oo, isa rin yun. Pero napakaganda, dapat ang mayor muna ang mauna. Sayang.' (Son of a b*tch, what a waste. They raped her, they lined up. I was angry because she was raped... But she was so beautiful, the mayor should have been first. What a waste.) -- CJ preserving the verbatim text without editorial comment, leaving readers to evaluate.

Poe's women quote: 'dapat mas maraming mga babae... ang bigyan ng pagkakataon sa gobyerno, sapagkat tayo ay nakakaramdam. Inaalagaan natin ang ating pamilya' (There should be more women given an opportunity to serve in government because we have empathy. We take care of our family) -- the antipodal contrast to Duterte's rape comment.

Robredo's defining vision quote: 'Isa po akong ina, at hindi ko po papabayaan iyong aking mga anak, hindi ko po papabayaan ang bayan' (I am a mother and I will not abandon my children, I will not abandon the country) -- captures the mother-as-leader register defining her campaign.
Marcos vision quote: 'leaders that seek to unite, not to divide, leaders that look to the future, not to the past' -- using parallel-construction-antithesis to position himself.

one_paragraph_summary: Panganiban applies a 'macho power vs woman power' frame to the 2016 PH presidential race -- observing that recent Pulse Asia and SWS surveys show Digong Duterte (DD) and Bongbong Marcos (BM) as the candidates to beat, with Grace Poe (GP) and Leni Robredo (LR) as the closest credible challengers. The two men, especially DD, are 'strong-willed, hyperbolic, magnetic, unorthodox and brash,' while the women are 'polished, compassionate, motherly, loving and humble.' Parenthetically, the same phenomenon appears in the US, where Trump and Clinton 'uncannily... typify the phenomenon of macho power vs woman power.' To demonstrate, CJ uses direct quotations across five policy domains. On peace and order, DD threatens 'it will be bloody because I will order the killing of all criminals... I will recommend to Congress the restoration of the death penalty by hanging in public,' while GP says 'As a mother, I am deeply troubled by the proliferation of crime and drugs. Like every parent, I cannot rest easy until my children are home safe at night.' On corruption, DD bets his life ('if I fail, kill me'); GP commits to hold the corrupt accountable 'whether they be friend or foe' and to push FOI legislation. On poverty alleviation, DD proposes food terminals, Land Bank lending to farmers, DTI-supported credit unions, and continuation/enhancement of 4Ps; GP says (in Tagalog) that alleviating poverty is her priority -- strengthening 4Ps and adding livelihood for additional income. On foreign relations, DD says 'We cannot afford to war with China' but vows to 'ride a jet ski carrying the Philippine flag' to a Chinese-occupied airport (Spratlys), and threatens to sever ties with America and Australia; GP advocates strengthening the military, constructive talks with China, and ASEAN leadership for a code of conduct. On women, DD's mayor-rape comment is preserved verbatim with Tagalog + English translation; GP says (in Tagalog) that more women should be in government because 'we have empathy' and care for family. The Marcos-Robredo VP race exhibits parallel contrasts: Marcos seeks 'leaders that seek to unite, not to divide, leaders that look to the future, not to the past,' aspiring to run DOLE (since employment is the biggest problem); Robredo identifies herself as 'a mother' refusing to abandon children or country, aspiring to streamline anti-poverty programs (not hold a cabinet position).
